paragraphs.text: Takayama et al. (2016) stated that mutations in the MEGF10 gene cause early-onset myopathy with areflexia, respiratory distress, and dysphagia (EMARDD), as well as a milder phenotype of minicore myopathy. Before their report, 6 families with EMARDD and 1 family with the milder disorder had been described. The mild variant is a congenital myopathy that resembles multiminicore disease. Weakness begins in infancy or childhood and is mainly axial and proximal, and patients have facial weakness, contractures, scoliosis, hypernasal speech or palatal abnormalities, and respiratory involvement starting later than in the severe form. Muscle biopsies show minicores and dystrophic or myofibrillar changes (Boyden et al., 2012; Croci et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) reported a nonconsanguineous Caucasian family of mixed European ancestry (family 1030) in which 3 of 4 sibs had an autosomal recessive myopathy that resembled multiminicore disease. Weakness began by 12 months of age, starting in the neck. It was mainly axial and proximal, included facial weakness, and stabilized in adolescence. Neck contractures appeared in infancy, and contractures of the elbows, knees, and heel cords had developed by adulthood. Serum creatine kinase (CK) was mildly elevated. All 3 patients had childhood-onset scoliosis treated with spinal fusion. From age 10 to 11 years, all 3 developed respiratory problems treated with nighttime bilevel positive airway pressure. All had hypernasal speech; 1 was born with a cleft palate, and another had a midline palatal ridge. Muscle biopsies had dystrophic features: myofibers replaced by fatty tissue, increased perimysial and endomysial connective tissue, and isolated regenerating fibers. The biopsies also showed moth-eaten fibers and minicores, suggesting a congenital myopathy. Rimmed vacuoles, inclusions, central cores, nemaline rods, and ragged red fibers were absent. Type I fibers slightly predominated, and fiber size varied markedly.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) also described a girl (subject 105-1) who had been diagnosed with multiminicore disease. She was a sporadic case of Caucasian background with distant Portuguese ancestry. She developed hypotonia with a weak neck at several weeks of age. She had a markedly high-arched palate, failure to thrive due to poor feeding, blue-tinged sclerae, hyperflexible joints, and frequent pulmonary infections, but no chronic breathing problems. Serum CK was mildly elevated at age 10 years. Mild scoliosis had progressed to 20 degrees by age 12. She had mild nonprogressive proximal and facial weakness. Muscle biopsy showed fiber size variation, internal nuclei, and minicores, and electron microscopy confirmed the minicores.

paragraphs.text: Croci et al. (2022) reported a 22-year-old Italian man, born to healthy consanguineous parents, who had a congenital myopathy with elbow contractures, scoliosis, and weak suck from the first months of life. He had no motor developmental delay or intellectual disability. He developed slowly progressive muscle weakness with impaired walking, rhinolalia, dysphagia, and respiratory involvement, and needed nocturnal noninvasive ventilation from age 16 years. Examination showed axial hypotonia, generalized muscle hypotrophy and weakness, preserved facial expression, cleft palate, global areflexia, and contractures of the elbows and ankles. Serum CK, brain and spine MRI, and cardiac studies were normal. He walked without support but with an equinovarus foot stance, hyperlordosis, and pelvic tilt, and needed a manual wheelchair for longer trips. He underwent bilateral Achilles tendon tenotomy and vertebral arthrodesis. From age 17 he had swallowing difficulties and recurrent pulmonary infections due to aspiration. Electrophysiologic studies showed normal motor and sensory conduction except for reduced compound muscle action potential amplitude. Sensation was not impaired. A quadriceps muscle biopsy at age 5 years showed nonspecific myopathic changes: variation in fiber size, internal nuclei, and fibrosis. A later second biopsy showed myofibrillar alterations, including whorled fibers, cytoplasmic inclusions, and minicores. The authors suggested that this pattern pointed to a myofibrillar myopathy and showed that the disease had progressed.

The affected sibs were compound heterozygous for 2 missense mutations in the MEGF10 gene: C326R in EGF-like domain 6 and C774R in EGF-like domain 16. Knockdown of megf10 in zebrafish caused a myopathic phenotype, which the authors took as support for the pathogenicity of the human mutations.

paragraphs.text: In a 22-year-old Italian man, born to consanguineous parents, with a progressive form of mild-variant EMARDD, Croci et al. (2022) used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous c.2096G-C transversion (NM_001256545.2) in the MEGF10 gene. The change predicts a cys699-to-ser (C699S) substitution at a conserved cysteine in an EGF-like domain. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the patient was homozygous, and both healthy parents were heterozygous carriers. The variant was absent from ClinVar and gnomAD and was predicted damaging by several in silico tools. It was classified as likely pathogenic under ACMG criteria. No functional studies were done.
